projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Howard M. Buchholz was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Howard M. Buchholz. Mr. Buchholz served in the U.S. Army. Howard served in the European theater and his highest rank was Staff Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Buchholz' home in North Olmstead, Ohio, on November 22nd, 2002. Howard was 81 at the time of this recording. Okay. Where were you living in 1941 when the war started for America?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I was in -- I wasn't married then yet. No, I was living in Michigan, I believe, because -- no, I was -- I -- I got married after I got out of the war. I was living in Michigan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In Michigan?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah. And I just went there and I was there, what, three years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor? Do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were you doing that day?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I was -- I still think I was a civilian. Oh, yes, I know I was, because I was with a church group.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: And we were having a play and the like. And we were all, oh, 17, 18 years old. And I thought, well -- and we all thought, oh, what a terrible thing it was, because we figured maybe by next month we wouldn't be there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: So, consequently, we all went in, a few at a time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you join?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. It was probably at least six months -- six months, at least.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sometime in 1942?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: And...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You joined the Army; is that right?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Well, I didn't join. They --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You got --

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They asked you to join?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. They didn't exactly stand -- or get on their hands and knees, but they asked me. You do or else.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: But, anyhow, that's what most of my friends went in. I sometimes think I should have joined the Navy. It was a little cleaner, --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: -- but -- then from there I went -- I don't know -- it was some -- well, the first place I went to, I think, was a -- on the West Coast. I forget the name of the Army. If I give it some thought, maybe I could think about it, but those are things I pretty much tried to forget. Oh, anyhow, I went to California. And then from California they sent me to Chicago to radio school. And I went to radio school where I learned the Morse code and stuff. But then they sent me to a -- an outfit in North Carolina which was an antiaircraft outfit. And I was a radioman there, but there wasn't much there. And most of our communications were done by field phones, anyhow. So then it -- oh, where did they send me? Oh, I forget what the other camp is. And then, oh, yeah, a real good commanding officer. He was -- he went -- he was a rich young man that went to military school, so we were all pretty much spic and span most of the time, especially at the inspections. But, consequently, I got to Europe and landed in England and that was -- I was there during Christmastime, I think. And then the -- the invasion came in and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: -- they pulled us into France.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you landed on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: D-Day plus?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: D-Day plus, yeah. No, I -- I got there and -- my outfit, I don't know whether they got there the day -- it wasn't but a day or so after. But my -- the landing craft I was on hit something in and we had a rough time getting in. Well, in the meantime, our -- our battalion vehicles left and here I was up the proverbial creek. And I just thought, well, what the heck. I'm just going to stay there. They'll come and look for me. And, you know, I think the second day they found out who I was. And I was getting to be worried because I figured here I'm missing in action, out two days, maybe they're -- they'd call my family and tell them I was missing, but I wasn't missing. They lost me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were stuck out there or did you --

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah. I was stuck -- no, I pulled into -- we pulled in --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just got separated from ____

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, we separated. And then, of course, they got -- they landed and they took out -- they had a designated place they were going and I didn't know where they were going, because I wasn't driving the truck and...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you stayed in that spot on the beach, huh?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, I stayed at that spot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that Utah Beach?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Huh? Gee, I don't know. Yeah, Utah. Utah Beach, that's it. I thought you said "you talk beach."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, I thought I had written down in the note that it was Utah Beach where you landed.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, Utah -- Utah Beach, but...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then they finally found you?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And, of course, then they had their radioman and so -- I mean, I -- I had my radio equipment and my -- and, of course, I also helped with the laying of phone lines, because I used to have a -- see, I had a T-4 rank, which was a -- a tech sergeant. And my -- my boss, of course, was just a buck sergeant. He just stood out a little, but, anyhow, he and I got along good. As a matter of fact, before we left the States, I visited at his home with him in New York. See, we were in New Jersey for a little while before we left. But those things are so far gone, I have a rough time remembering the easy things now. But we did -- we were pretty active and, as I say, a dozen medals. It shows that we were there, --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: -- if nothing else. I would pretty much feel that I never killed anybody, so -- and they didn't bother me and I didn't bother them. And I could speak German.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day when -- in combat over there after you landed?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Gee, they -- we were just glad to -- oh, I didn't -- it was about, what was it, two or three days after, so -- I mean, we just had the -- the local things to do. Being a -- a field -- I mean, an antiaircraft outfit, they used us quite a bit as a field piece that we could -- so -- but I never had any combat myself. I was on the radio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were on the radio. So what would -- your job would be communications, laying wire and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Well, yeah, I was a -- well, I was a communication sergeant.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: And I -- I -- I was -- the regular communication sergeant was just a -- a private first class or a private -- or -- not -- maybe not a private. He was a sergeant. I was a tech sergeant. But I didn't have any -- I -- well, I liked being there for the little time I was there and then we -- we even helped -- helped them, I think, with a little bit of antiaircraft fire when they were -- and then we -- we were -- that was around Christmastime and we -- I think the invasion wasn't around even -- it was around spring, was -- I -- I don't --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think it was about six months later.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh. So consequently I don't have any fond memories of the service, but I'm glad I was able to take part.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you were in England, did you spend much time with the British people?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Oh, I had a nice girlfriend.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah. And, a matter of fact, I think -- and we were decent. I can think of it that way. I think it was in the fact that she -- after the war, she didn't ____ probably anyhow. And once I left England, I heard from her off and on, but never went back. But, no, I had -- and the -- the family liked me there. They even had me there for dinners and stuff. And they were on a pretty strict diet there. And sometimes I'd go over and I -- I forget what her -- sometimes I only remember her -- her last name, but, jeez, that's -- that's a long time ago. And things were rationed there and stuff. Sometimes I'd go there for dinner and she'd say, "Howard, I have something you might like." And the -- the mother -- they liked me pretty good. I was a decent man and they had a decent daughter, so, consequently, I enjoyed my stay in England. And having a little bit of rank, I got a little bit -- well, I had a little bit more leeway. I could go different places, and the like. So I put out the war. I had a brother that was in it and he -- I left -- well, he was in the -- the service before I went in and I visited him before I left and -- and I don't know whether he even got to go overseas because he was -- oh, I think he was about ten years older than me, but, anyhow.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies in the outfit?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Oh, yeah, uh-huh. Yeah. As a matter of fact, our communication sergeant was -- his last name was Seigel, Bill Seigel. And I spent the -- when we were still in Jersey, I spent the weekend at his house in New England. No, he and I were good buddies, but after the war and the like we split up and -- and he was in -- I mean, he was -- with the wires in our outfit, but, I mean, after the ____but I try to forget as much as possible. I don't like to talk too much about it. I'm no hero. I did a good job, I think, and they were satisfied. They paid me and they -- actually, they give me a little raise when I left. They give me an extra stripe and I got -- it's a -- what's it? It was the -- three stripes and, what was it -- master sergeant or something. Yeah, master sergeant. So Uncle Sam gave me a raise. They were glad to get rid of me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever get any shows or do anything for entertainment when you had a break?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Not very much, no. They used to have some right near, but, no, I -- I was more or less a loner, I guess. Well, I had a good -- the fellow that became our -- my sergeant, you know, Bill Seigel, he and I were -- well, I don't -- my two best buddies were Jews, but...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So where did you go after D-Day? Where did your outfit go?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: After D-Day. I stayed there for -- oh, we had to stay there for more or less military police and I worked in the office down there, pretty much. But they have to -- had to get people that used to pilfer things and steal -- and we -- we took over like, more or less. That's so -- I can't remember what it was like anymore, because it's so faded. But I know we did stay in France for a bit. And then the thing is we're glad because the Japanese were still out, but...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your outfit? What was the number?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I don't know if I could ever look around anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: It was a AAA, --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: -- antiaircraft artillery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you -- was your outfit involved in the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, they pulled us in. But we were good support, you know. Not me, I didn't -- I didn't ever fire my gun. I had a radio to...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: But I -- yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I don't remember particularly. I mean, there -- that's something -- that's something real serious, but -- oh, I -- it's been so long. I try to forget as much as I can. I certainly don't think this interview is much good to you, because I just -- I got a good memory, but it's short. I keep -- I keep telling people I sometimes wonder who that old man is I shave when I get up in the morning. And I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think of the Army food?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Pretty good. As a matter of fact, I was from Michigan and the -- the head cook there was from Michigan, too. And so he took care of these Michiganders, so -- no, the Army is okay. I wouldn't recommend it to anybody, but I was very fortunate and so was my brother. He was a couple years older than me, but I don't know what he was with. But I thought I was very unfortunate -- or very fortunate, being in the antiaircraft, because we didn't have any air -- air attacks at our place.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: But funny --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: The funny thing that did happen, though, is when the headquarters pulled in on Omaha Beach and left, I was stranded, but in my truck -- in -- there was the -- one of the -- I think the -- one of the -- the lieutenant's sleeping bags. And, by God, we -- I did was just keep rolled up in my Army blanket. I thought, "I'm here and it's mine until he finds out where it went." But evidently he found it. I -- he never arrested me for anything. Actually, most of them missed me. I was a good soldier, I thought, but -- but I had a very strong faith in God and I tried as much as possible to never miss a -- a service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The --

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: What do you call it, the Army minister, you know?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, the chaplain?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, the chaplain. As a matter of fact, I -- as a matter of fact, I did convert a couple guys, but -- but, anything, that's -- those days are gone. I don't like to remember them much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters and packages from home?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would they send?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Gee, I don't know. My mother or, yes, my mother, I wasn't married, and she used to send something. I don't know, cookies or something, maybe she'd cook some, but that's a hard thing to remember. I -- I wasn't married or anything, but my mother was -- would send me things. But, all and all, the war wasn't so good. It was better than none at all, though. That's -- that's right, what was it in the song? It came out, a song, "The Army isn't so good, but it's" -- or "the war isn't so good, but it's better than none at all."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't remember that one.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: But, anyhow.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. It wasn't -- it wasn't too long after the -- the Japs give in. At -- at least I think they gave in. I think that was after the atomic bomb, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: And...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember celebrating either VE-Day or VJ-Day?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Not particularly. I think I told you what happened to me in Germany, though.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Say that again.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I did learn -- I went to a German Lutheran school. I learned to read it. I'm not ___ and I was in the command post one day and the -- that's when I had my ___ ready. He says, "Sergeant, know anybody that can read German?" I said, "Yes, sir, I can read German as well as I can read English." And I just went down that thing. And he said, "Hey, that's marvelous." He says, "What does that say?" I said, "Sir, I can read it, but I can't understand it." And he says, "Get the hell out of here." He says, "You're crazy." And as I left the command post, he said to the lieutenant, "Remember," he says, "just think of it, he can read the goddamn stuff, but can't understand it." But we had a medic, his parents were German, he understood German, so I could -- I could read it to him and he -- he said it's like -- what -- what it was anymore, yeah. He satisfied the captain.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why couldn't you understand it? Was it just jumbled or --

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Well, the thing is, German is not really easy, because there's "der, die" and "das." I mean, "der" is male and "die" is woman and "das" is pretty much feminine. But then it's -- then it's hard to -- to distinguish even -- oh -- oh, I don't know. There -- there was some mistake, so I learned -- I learned enough. I could get by with it and never ___in Germany, because all my grandparents were born in Germany. My -- my parents were born there, but -- but I -- I -- they used to have a song the war was a terrible -- I mean, but still was better than nothing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you think -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I wouldn't join, but I'm glad -- well, my son did have to go in, more or less, in the National Guard or something, because, boy, he's no kid anymore, either. He's over 50.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: So...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah. And this was right near the end of the war, not too far -- I don't know where we -- and one of the friends -- my friends that was lying in the -- my battery, then he was transferred to headquarters. And one day he came to visit me where we were and on his way back home, you know how these Germans where they used to plant a wire across the streets, he was going home in the jeep with a driver, of course, and he hit -- got hit and he was decapitated. So from then on I thought, gee, you know, I might be German, but most of those Germans are very nice -- aren't very nice people. And they started it; that's the thing, but -- oh, it was a good experience. I mean, really, I got those five or -- or three -- three or -- no, there's four major battles. I know Normandy was there and, of course, some of the other ones. It was a big thing. Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Served in the Battle of the Bulge and the --

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And the battles in Germany.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, I mean, there -- there were four of them that I -- I got...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Battle stars?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Battle stars. So I wasn't -- well, lonesome, but -- oh, and I had gotten up -- when I finally left it, I was -- I finally left, I think, as staff sergeant, so I must have did a good job.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: And I had -- I had some good guys I worked with. Some of them were from Brooklyn and the Bronx and a little -- oh, uncultured, I would say. Well, I -- there's not too much culture in the Army, anyhow, but -- but I did have some good friends and, of course, most of them by now are dead because there's -- matter of fact, two of my best friends -- oh, I ___ as a matter of fact this fellow from New Jersey. And I think at one time when my wife was in New Jersey, I think we even stopped and visited. Like they used to say, it's a terrible thing, as I recall, but still it's better than none at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: I would have been pretty lonesome at home anyhow with everybody else gone.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All the guys are gone, huh?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Yeah, but that was all. I hope you have a little bit on your ___ that it can help, but it's just stuff. I'm a rather religious person and God's watched over me very much and basically speaking, of course, I was progressively a godly person. I prayed a lot, went to -- you know, I didn't have any -- any intimate problems, so -- no problems that plagued me but I don't know. No, I mean, I -- I told my folks when I got in the service I behaved, and I think I did. They were glad to see me home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You got that. Do you remember that reunion when you got home?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Oh, pretty much so. Not -- well, I had a brother that came home, too. Of course, they were glad to see him. The only thing is that he'd got married while he was in the Army. He got married before he was sent overseas. She didn't like to see their kids getting married, I guess, so...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have a party when you got back?

sp.speaker: Howard M. Buchholz
sp.p: Not that I know of, no. My mother might have had a good home-baked bread and a nice roast chicken or something, but, no, we were never much of a family for even, oh -- or celebrating birthdays and stuff. It was just another day. (END OF TAPE.)
